 About What might it mean to live a flourishing life? And what is the relationship between flourishing and the virtues, especially justice? In this talk based on her recent book, Professor Angie Hobbs explores how Plato can help us with these urgent questions, and how he addresses the key issue of character formation, and why it never benefits us to return wrong for wrong. She shows how she has used his methodology, ideas and arguments in a variety of sectors to address contemporary issues in education, faith–secular debate, health care and the civil service, and invites the audience to discuss with her what further lessons can be applied. We are living in fast-moving and uncertain times and need ancient wisdom more than ever. Plato really does matter, right now!

 Situations in which claims to authority clash with each other abound in international law, ranging from competition for authority among international adjudicative bodies to the disputed allocation of powers among international and domestic authorities across various issue areas.  About 

 Abstract : Consent has famously been described as moral magic because of its purported power to transform otherwise wrongful sexual contact into permissible conduct. On this “transformative” view, a person’s consent changes what others may permissibly do, at least sometimes allowing sex to occur even when it’s expected to make the consenter significantly worse off. I defend an alternative. Under the “evidential” view, consent is a proxy for a person’s welfare. It is our best indicator of how sexual contact is likely to affect that person’s welfare.  About In Memoriam Andreas von Hirsch (1934-2026) 
 The Institute of Criminology is indebted to Andreas von Hirsch in many and profound ways. We will mention just three. First, because he was a valued member of the Institute for many years; second because he was an extraordinarily generous benefactor; and third because he was a towering intellectual figure in his own right. He was a pioneering force in taking seriously the connections between criminology and related fields – and both criminology and those other fields are much enriched by the interdisciplinary relationships his work contributed so decisively to emphasise. His work at the helm of the Committee for the Study of Incarceration (1976) continues to reward rereading – so much so that another workshop devoted to Doing Justice (the final “Report” of that Committee) is planned for 3-4 December (and had been planned before news of his passing reached its organizers). “Justice matters”, von Hirsch emphasised throughout his career: and it is a matter of justice – but also of immense gratitude – that we honour him with this memorial.

events.title: Counterfeit Procedure: How 'Digital Arrest' Fraud Simulates the State
events.venue: Webinar & Lecture Theatre 2, Computer Laboratory, William Gates Building
events.speaker: Shakti Avasthy, Indian Police Service
events.description:
In the fraud known in India as 'digital arrest', victims are told by people posing as officers of several state agencies that they are under investigation, shown forged orders of the country's highest court, held under continuous video 'custody' for days, and instructed to move their savings into a 'supervised' account for verification. Recorded complaints rose from about 40,000 in 2022 to over 120,000 in 2024. This talk argues that the offence is not impersonation but institutional simulation: what the operators reproduce is not a person but the procedural form by which a state proceeds against a citizen - inter-agency referral, documentary authority, staged adjudication, custody - closely enough that compliance follows from recognising the procedure rather than believing any individual. Victims who verify are captured by the act of verifying. Drawing on one case reconstructed from the investigative record of a police commissionerate in India's National Capital Region, and six comparator cases from the public record, the talk sets out the architecture, the inversion of the burden of proof that makes it durable, and why the single most effective state intervention observed was not an arrest campaign but a public statement of a procedure the state never uses. It closes on the uncomfortable corollary: because the fraud borrows real authority rather than inventing it, its power rises with the capability of the state it imitates.

events.title: CFL/Cambridge Socio-Legal Group Seminar: 'The evolution of parenthood in Brazil: from the single-parent stigma to multiple parenthood'
events.venue: Faculty of Law, David Williams Building
events.description:

 1:00pm to 2:00pm

 Location: 

 Faculty of Law, David Williams Building

 G24

 About 

 Speaker: Professor João Costa-Neto (University of Brasília)
 Abstract: Brazilian family law has undergone a remarkable transformation: from a system built around marriage, biological descent and exclusive parenthood to one increasingly willing to recognise families as they are actually lived. This talk will trace that evolution, focusing on the rise of socioaffective parenthood and the idea that being a parent may result not only from biology, but also from care, responsibility and the social reality of family life. It then explores the most striking consequence of that shift: multiple parenthood, under which biological and socioaffective parents may coexist with equal legal status. Drawing on constitutional change, legal scholarship and recent case law, we will understand how Brazil moved from debating who the “real” parent is to accepting that, in some families, there may be more than one.
 This event is a hybrid event. If you are in Cambridge, please do join us in the Faculty. To attend online you must register via Zoom .

Speaker: Professor Andrés Rodríguez-Pose
 Talk Title: The two geographies of artificial intelligence: AI invention, AI use and regional economic performance in Europe
 Time: 18:00 -19:30 
 Location: Ramsden room, St Catharine's College 
 The seminar series is supported by the Cambridge Political Economy Society and the Economics and Policy Group at the Cambridge Judge Business School. 

 Talk Overview: :
 Artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to raise economic performance. Much less is known about where in Europe its economic returns land. This article distinguishes between AI invention —the creation of new AI technologies— and AI use —their deployment in production— and asks which of the two is associated with regional economic performance. AI invention is measured through AI patent applications and AI use through AI labor demand, the number of AI-skill mentions per 1,000 online job advertisements, drawn from Cedefop’s Skills-OVATE data and validated against firm-level adoption. Because hiring and growth are jointly determined, regional AI labor demand is instrumented with a shift-share prediction based on pre-period industrial structure and national trends in AI hiring by sector. Estimates for 191 European NUTS-2 regions over 2022–2024 reveal a clear asymmetry. Regions with higher AI labor demand grew faster in GDP per capita and labor productivity, with no detectable change in employment. AI patenting shows no association with growth. The two geographies barely overlap:

events.description:
Date/time: 

 Friday 12 February 2027 

 4:00pm to 5:00pm

 Location: 

 David Attenborough Building

 About 

 Speaker: Dr Rhiannon Ogden-Jones (University of Cambridge)
 The Cambridge Seminar Series on Law and the Climate Crisis explores the vital role of legal systems in tackling one of the most pressing issues of our time.
 This series brings together top experts in law and climate action to discuss how climate change interacts with specific areas of law, setting out both how legal fields are being impacted by climate change and how the law can help drive climate action.
 The Cambridge Seminar Series on Law and the Climate Crisis is co-hosted by the Centre for Climate Engagement at Hughes Hall, Cambridge Zero, the Centre for Environment, Energy and Natural Resource Governance (CEENRG), the Cambridge Climate Society, the Lauterpacht Centre for International Law, and the Net Zero Lawyers Alliance.
 For more information and to register see the Centre for Climate Engagement website .

events.title: Writing Policy Impact into Funding Applications
events.venue: West Hub, JJ Thomson Ave, Cambridge CB3 0US
events.speaker: CSaP
events.description:
A workshop from CSaP and Cambridge Reproduction
 Join the Centre for Science and Policy (CSaP) and Cambridge Reproduction's Policy and Reproductive Justice Theme for an interactive workshop exploring how researchers can identify, develop and communicate the policy relevance of their work.
 Funders increasingly expect researchers to demonstrate how their research may inform policy, influence practice, or contribute to societal outcomes. This workshop will help participants understand what policy impact looks like in practice and how to effectively articulate policy pathways and outcomes within funding applications.
 Through practical examples, case studies and interactive discussion, participants will explore approaches to policy engagement, learn how research can contribute to policy development, and gain tools for incorporating policy impact into project design from the outset.
 The workshop will cover: 
 Understanding policy impact and why it matters to funders
 Identifying relevant policy audiences, stakeholders and opportunities for engagement
 Developing realistic and credible pathways to policy outcomes
 Articulating policy relevance and impact effectively in grant applications
 Learning from examples of successful policy engagement in reproductive research and beyond
 The session is open to researchers at all career stages and from all disciplines, from those new to policy engagement to those looking to strengthen the policy dimensions of their funding applications and
